Dyshemoglobinemias

Tintinalli Ch.207 + CO Ch.222 + Rosen Cyanosis/Cyanide — COHb, MetHb, SulfHb, Cyanide

Emergency Medicine Board Review

Thai EM BoardTintinalliRosen'sToxicology chapter

Introduction: Cyanosis That Oxygen Does Not Fix

Fast Frame

Dyshemoglobinemia = hemoglobin present but not carrying/releasing oxygen normally. Main ED buckets: carboxyhemoglobin, methemoglobin, sulfhemoglobin, and cyanide as a related cellular oxygen-use poison.

COPulse ox falsely normal; CO-oximetry needed; treat with 100% O2 +/- HBO.
MetHbCyanosis, chocolate blood, saturation gap; methylene blue if symptomatic or >25%.
SulfHbCyanosis, pulse ox falsely low, does not respond to methylene blue.
CyanideCellular hypoxia: severe lactic acidosis, shock, coma after smoke/fire/industrial exposure.
Rosen source check

Cyanosis Algorithm

Rosen starts from bedside cyanosis: peripheral vs central, response to oxygen, then CO-oximetry/methemoglobin testing. Useful before jumping to antidotes.

Rosen vs Tintinalli: Rosen adds a bedside diagnostic fork before the antidote algorithm; Tintinalli remains the treatment spine.

Carbon Monoxide: Carboxyhemoglobin

Pattern

CO binds hemoglobin with very high affinity, shifts oxyhemoglobin curve left, and impairs mitochondrial oxygen use. The danger is tissue hypoxia with a deceptively normal pulse oximeter.

Tintinalli source check

CO Sources, Curve, Symptoms, HBO Indications

Use source history + symptoms. COHb level helps confirm exposure but does not perfectly predict severity, especially after oxygen has already been given.

Board Trap

Standard pulse oximetry cannot distinguish oxyhemoglobin from carboxyhemoglobin. A “normal SpO2” does not rule out CO poisoning. Order CO-oximetry.

Methemoglobinemia: Ferric Hemoglobin

Tintinalli source check

MetHb Mechanism and Causes

MetHb is Hb(Fe3+) that cannot bind oxygen. Remaining normal hemoglobin holds oxygen more tightly, worsening tissue hypoxia.

Recognition

  • Cyanosis not improving with oxygen.
  • Pulse ox often stuck around ~85% regardless of PaO2.
  • ABG PaO2 can be normal/high: oxygen dissolved in plasma is fine, hemoglobin carriage is not.
  • Chocolate-brown blood is classic.
  • Confirm by co-oximetry with methemoglobin percentage.
Tintinalli source check

Treatment Approach

Tintinalli recommends methylene blue for symptomatic patients or MetHb >25%, with supportive care and decontamination as needed.

Methylene Blue Failure

Think G6PD deficiency, NADPH-methemoglobin reductase deficiency, hemoglobin M, sulfhemoglobinemia, chlorate/dapsone ongoing oxidant stress, or inadequate dose/decontamination.

Sulfhemoglobinemia: Rare, Persistent Cyanosis

How It Differs

Sulfhemoglobin is irreversible and persists for the lifespan of the red cell. It can look like methemoglobinemia clinically, but does not improve with methylene blue.

Management is mostly supportive; severe toxicity may require exchange transfusion or packed RBC transfusion depending on the case.

Cyanide: Cellular Oxygen Use Failure

Pattern

Cyanide blocks mitochondrial cytochrome oxidase, so cells cannot use oxygen. Suspect in smoke inhalation with coma/shock/severe lactic acidosis, industrial exposure, or nitroprusside toxicity.

Rosen source check

Box 148.2. Cyanide Antidotes

Rosen gives practical cyanide antidote dosing and a key warning: nitrites induce methemoglobinemia, so avoid/withhold nitrites when COHb is elevated, such as fire victims.

Rosen vs Tintinalli: Rosen makes the nitrite/COHb conflict explicit; Tintinalli anchors the broader dyshemoglobinemia management sequence.

Fire Victim Logic

Smoke inhalation can mean both CO and cyanide. Hydroxocobalamin is preferred because it does not worsen oxygen-carrying capacity, unlike nitrite-induced methemoglobinemia.

Key Points: Dyshemoglobinemias

Pulse Ox Trap

CO can have normal SpO2. MetHb often sits around ~85%. Use co-oximetry.

Saturation Gap

Normal/high PaO2 on ABG with low pulse ox suggests dyshemoglobinemia.

CO

Treat immediately with 100% O2; consider HBO for neurologic/cardiac/pregnancy/severe features.

MetHb

Chocolate blood + cyanosis not responsive to O2. Treat symptomatic or >25% with methylene blue.

G6PD

Methylene blue needs NADPH pathway; G6PD deficiency raises failure/hemolysis risk.

Dapsone

Can cause prolonged/recurrent MetHb due active metabolite; repeat dosing and cimetidine may be considered.

Cyanide

Severe lactate/shock/coma after smoke inhalation: give hydroxocobalamin early.

Nitrite Warning

Nitrites create MetHb; bad fit for fire victims with possible COHb.

Inline Assessment MCQs

Q1. A 35-year-old firefighter is rescued from a structure fire. He is confused and has a headache. Pulse oximetry reads 98%. Arterial blood gas shows PaO2 95 mmHg and SaO2 (calculated) 97%. What is the most likely diagnosis and what is the critical diagnostic discrepancy?
  • A. Opioid intoxication — naloxone should be given empirically
  • B. Carbon monoxide poisoning — pulse oximetry is falsely normal because it cannot distinguish COHb from oxyHb
  • C. Methemoglobinemia — treat with methylene blue immediately
  • D. Normal evaluation — confusion is from smoke inhalation irritants only
❌ Incorrect. While confusion can occur with opioids, the firefighter context strongly suggests CO poisoning. Pulse oximetry reads normal with CO poisoning, masking the true diagnosis.
✅ Correct. CO causes SpO2 to read falsely normal (COHb absorbs like oxyHb at 660 nm). Co-oximetry measuring COHb directly is required. The 'saturation gap' between SpO2 and true saturation is diagnostic.
❌ Incorrect. Methemoglobinemia would cause SpO2 to plateau at ~85% (MetHb reads as ~85% regardless of concentration). The normal SpO2 reading and fire context point to CO, not methemoglobin.
❌ Incorrect. CO poisoning causes tissue hypoxia despite adequate lung function. Normal SpO2 and PaO2 in a confused firefighter must raise CO poisoning as the primary concern.
Q2. A 52-year-old receives dapsone for dermatitis herpetiformis. He develops progressive dyspnea and is found to have SpO2 of 83% on 15L non-rebreather mask. ABG shows PaO2 of 290 mmHg. What is the diagnosis and initial treatment?
  • A. Severe ARDS — intubate and provide PEEP ventilation
  • B. Carbon monoxide poisoning — 100% O2 via non-rebreather mask
  • C. Methemoglobinemia from dapsone — methylene blue 1-2 mg/kg IV
  • D. Pulmonary embolism — anticoagulate immediately
❌ Incorrect. PaO2 of 290 mmHg on 15L O2 indicates excellent gas exchange. Low SpO2 with high PaO2 is the classic dyshemoglobinemia pattern, not ARDS.
❌ Incorrect. CO poisoning causes falsely NORMAL SpO2. This patient has LOW SpO2 with high PaO2, which is the methemoglobinemia pattern. Also dapsone is a classic cause of MetHb.
✅ Correct. Dapsone causes MetHb. The SpO2-PaO2 gap (PaO2 290 but SpO2 83%) is diagnostic. MetHb causes SpO2 to plateau at ~85%. Methylene blue reduces MetHb by enhancing the NADPH-dependent methemoglobin reductase pathway.
❌ Incorrect. PE would not cause MetHb pattern (SpO2 plateau at 85% with high PaO2). PE causes reduced PaO2 from V/Q mismatch, not the dyshemoglobin pattern.

Thai EM Board MCQs

Q1. ผู้ป่วยหญิงอายุ 28 ปี มีอาการปวดศีรษะ คลื่นไส้ และ confusion หลังนอนในบ้านที่ปิดสนิทพร้อมกับเตาถ่าน SpO2 99% HR 110 ผิวหน้าแดง ABG แสดง PaO2 88 mmHg ข้อใดเป็นสิ่งที่ต้องส่งตรวจทันที?
  • A. CT brain เพื่อหา intracranial hemorrhage
  • B. Co-oximetry บน arterial blood เพื่อวัด COHb โดยตรง
  • C. Urine drug screen เพื่อหา CO metabolite
  • D. Chest X-ray เพื่อดู pulmonary edema จาก CO
❌ ผิด. แม้จะทำ CT brain ได้ในภายหลัง แต่ CO poisoning ต้องวินิจฉัยก่อนด้วย co-oximetry การวินิจฉัยและรักษา CO poisoning เร็วสำคัญกว่า imaging
✅ ถูก. Pulse oximetry ผิดพลาดใน CO poisoning Co-oximetry วัดที่ 4+ wavelengths และแยก COHb, MetHb, oxyHb, deoxyHb ได้ถูกต้อง COHb >25% = severe poisoning
❌ ผิด. CO ไม่มี urine metabolite ที่วัดได้ด้วย UDS standard การวัด COHb ทำที่ blood เท่านั้น
❌ ผิด. CXR ไม่ช่วยวินิจฉัย CO poisoning การรักษา (100% O2) ควรเริ่มก่อน imaging ตามข้อบ่งชี้ทางคลินิก
Q2. ผู้ป่วยชายอายุ 60 ปี ได้รับการวินิจฉัย CO poisoning (COHb 35%) ถูกส่งมาที่ห้องฉุกเฉิน ข้อใดเป็นเกณฑ์ที่ทำให้ต้องพิจารณา Hyperbaric Oxygen (HBO) therapy?
  • A. COHb >5% ในผู้ป่วยทุกราย
  • B. ปวดศีรษะและคลื่นไส้เท่านั้น (mild poisoning)
  • C. Loss of consciousness, COHb >25%, neurological deficits, หรือ cardiac involvement
  • D. ผู้ป่วยสูบบุหรี่ทุกราย เพราะ baseline COHb สูงอยู่แล้ว
❌ ผิด. COHb >5% ไม่ใช่ข้อบ่งชี้ HBO ผู้ไม่สูบบุหรี่ปกติมี COHb 0-3%, ผู้สูบบุหรี่มีสูงถึง 10% COHb ระดับต่ำโดยไม่มีอาการไม่ต้องการ HBO
❌ ผิด. Mild symptoms (headache, nausea) โดยไม่มี LOC, neurological deficits, หรือ cardiac involvement โดยทั่วไปรักษาด้วย NBO 100% O2 เท่านั้น
✅ ถูก. HBO indications ที่ยอมรับกันส่วนใหญ่ได้แก่ LOC (ทุก duration), COHb >25%, neurological findings (seizure, focal deficits, cerebellar signs), cardiac toxicity, และ pregnancy (COHb >15-20%)
❌ ผิด. การสูบบุหรี่เองไม่ใช่ข้อบ่งชี้ HBO ต้องมีอาการเข้าข่ายข้างต้นจึงจะพิจารณา
Q3. ผู้ป่วยหญิงอายุ 22 ปี กิน nitrite ในยาเม็ด (amyl nitrite) SpO2 82% PaO2 310 mmHg ผิวหน้าออกน้ำตาล-เทา ข้อใดเป็นขั้นตอนการรักษาที่ถูกต้อง?
  • A. Sodium thiosulfate IV เพื่อ convert MetHb เป็น sulfhemoglobin
  • B. Hydroxocobalamin IV เพื่อ chelate MetHb
  • C. Exchange transfusion เป็น first-line treatment ในทุกกรณี
  • D. Methylene blue 1-2 mg/kg IV ช้าๆ — reduces MetHb ผ่าน NADPH-dependent pathway
❌ ผิด. Sodium thiosulfate ใช้สำหรับ cyanide poisoning ไม่ใช่ methemoglobinemia Sulfhemoglobin ไม่ใช่ผลที่ต้องการ
❌ ผิด. Hydroxocobalamin ใช้สำหรับ cyanide poisoning (chelates CN⁻) ไม่ใช่ methemoglobinemia
❌ ผิด. Exchange transfusion เป็น last resort สำหรับ refractory MetHb ใน G6PD deficiency ที่ methylene blue ไม่ได้ผล ไม่ใช่ first-line
✅ ถูก. Methylene blue เป็น first-line antidote สำหรับ symptomatic methemoglobinemia Mechanism: MB + NADPH (จาก G6PD pathway) → leukomethylene blue → reduces Fe³⁺ MetHb → Fe²⁺ Hb ปกติ
Q4. ผู้ป่วยที่มี G6PD deficiency ได้รับ methylene blue 2 mg/kg สำหรับ methemoglobinemia แต่ MetHb ไม่ลดลง สิ่งใดต่อไปนี้อธิบายเหตุการณ์นี้และวิธีจัดการที่ถูกต้อง?
  • A. G6PD deficiency ทำให้ขาด NADPH ซึ่งจำเป็นสำหรับ methylene blue — พิจารณา ascorbic acid หรือ exchange transfusion
  • B. Methylene blue dose ต่ำเกินไป ควรเพิ่มเป็น 10 mg/kg
  • C. ผู้ป่วยมี sulfhemoglobinemia ซึ่งไม่ตอบสนองต่อ methylene blue
  • D. รอ spontaneous resolution เพราะ MetHb จะลดลงเองใน 24 ชั่วโมง
✅ ถูก. G6PD pathway สร้าง NADPH ซึ่งจำเป็น ถ้าขาด G6PD → ขาด NADPH → methylene blue ไม่ reduce เป็น leukomethylene blue → ไม่มีประสิทธิภาพ Ascorbic acid เป็น alternative (slow-acting) Exchange transfusion เป็น definitive alternative
❌ ผิด. การเพิ่ม dose ไม่ช่วยใน G6PD deficiency เพราะ NADPH ไม่เพียงพออยู่แล้ว Methylene blue ในขนาดสูงยังทำให้เกิด methemoglobinemia ได้เองด้วย
❌ ผิด. Sulfhemoglobin ไม่ตอบสนองต่อ methylene blue จริง แต่ sulfhemoglobinemia เกิดจาก sulfonamides, metoclopramide ไม่ใช่ nitrite ปัญหาหลักในกรณีนี้คือ G6PD deficiency
❌ ผิด. MetHb >30% ทำให้เกิด severe hypoxia ได้ ในผู้ป่วยที่ไม่ตอบสนองต่อ methylene blue ต้องให้ treatment ทางเลือก ไม่ใช่รอ

Thai EM Board — InTraining Exam MCQs

Q1. A 45-year-old industrial worker was exposed to hydrogen cyanide gas after a chemical spill. He was found unconscious at the scene and brought to the ED with HR 45, BP 70/40, GCS 6, and lactic acidosis (lactate 18 mmol/L). EMS administered amyl nitrite pearls en route. What is the most appropriate definitive antidote treatment?
  • A. Sodium nitrite 300 mg IV followed by sodium thiosulfate 12.5g IV
  • B. Hydroxocobalamin 5g IV over 15 minutes (Cyanokit)
  • C. Supportive care only — lactic acidosis will resolve with IV fluids
  • D. High-dose oxygen via non-rebreather mask to displace cyanide from cytochrome c oxidase
❌ Incorrect as most appropriate. While the nitrite-thiosulfate combination works, it is less preferred in fire victims with potential CO poisoning because sodium nitrite produces methemoglobin, compounding the oxygen-carrying deficit from CO. Hydroxocobalamin is preferred.
✅ Correct. Hydroxocobalamin chelates cyanide to form cyanocobalamin (vitamin B12), which is eliminated renally. It does not produce methemoglobin, making it safe for fire victims with possible concurrent CO poisoning. Dose: 5g IV (70 mg/kg in children).
❌ Incorrect. Cyanide-induced lactic acidosis results from cellular metabolic arrest (cytochrome oxidase inhibition), not tissue underperfusion. IV fluids alone cannot correct cellular hypoxia; antidotal therapy is essential.
❌ Incorrect. While 100% O2 is given as adjunctive therapy, it does not significantly displace CN from cytochrome c oxidase at normal atmospheric pressure. Specific antidotal therapy is required.

McGraw-Hill Specialty Board Review MCQs

Q1. A patient with suspected CO poisoning is placed on a 100% non-rebreather mask. What is the effect of 100% normobaric oxygen on CO elimination?
  • A. 100% O2 has no effect on CO elimination rate
  • B. 100% O2 increases CO half-life from 20 minutes to 4 hours
  • C. 100% O2 reduces CO half-life from ~5 hours to ~60-90 minutes by mass-action displacement
  • D. 100% O2 is contraindicated in CO poisoning as it competes with CO for cytochrome binding
CO elimination follows first-order kinetics and is critically dependent on the inspired oxygen concentration. On room air (FiO2 21%), CO half-life is approximately 4-5 hours. Breathing 100% oxygen via non-rebreather mask (NBO) reduces the half-life to approximately 60-90 minutes. Hyperbaric oxygen (100% O2 at 2-3 ATA) further reduces the half-life to approximately 20-30 minutes by mass-action displacement of CO from hemoglobin and improved dissolved O2 delivery to tissues.
Q2. A 28-year-old with nitrate-induced methemoglobinemia is treated with methylene blue. His MetHb level was 42% before treatment. Which laboratory artifact should the physician be aware of regarding pulse oximetry after treatment?
  • A. Pulse oximetry will immediately normalize to 99% after methylene blue
  • B. Methylene blue causes pulse oximetry to falsely read approximately 65% for up to 2 hours
  • C. Pulse oximetry will read 100% after methylene blue because all MetHb is instantly reduced
  • D. Pulse oximetry is unaffected by methylene blue and can be used to monitor treatment
Methylene blue itself absorbs light at 668 nm (similar to the red wavelength used by pulse oximetry) and causes pulse oximetry to falsely read approximately 65% SpO2 for up to 1-2 hours after administration, even as the MetHb is successfully being reduced. This is a known artifact. Clinical assessment and serial co-oximetry (not pulse oximetry) should be used to monitor treatment response.
Q3. Which feature of cyanide poisoning distinguishes it from other causes of lactic acidosis (e.g., septic shock)?
  • A. Elevated venous PO2 (arterialization) despite severe lactic acidosis from impaired cellular oxygen utilization
  • B. Markedly reduced arterial PO2 from pulmonary toxicity
  • C. Presence of cherry-red skin uniquely found only in cyanide poisoning
  • D. Bradycardia is universally present in cyanide poisoning but absent in other lactic acidosis
Cyanide inhibits cytochrome c oxidase (Complex IV), blocking the electron transport chain and forcing all energy production through anaerobic glycolysis. This produces profound lactic acidosis. The distinguishing feature: despite severe lactic acidosis, the venous PO2 (or SvO2) is ELEVATED because cells cannot extract oxygen (oxygen is delivered but cannot be used). In septic shock and other circulatory causes of lactic acidosis, venous PO2 is LOW because oxygen is consumed peripherally but delivery is impaired. 'Arterialization of venous blood' is the hallmark of cellular poisoning.
Q4. A firefighter is found in a burning building with CO poisoning (COHb 28%) and is 22 weeks pregnant. She has a headache but is neurologically intact. Which statement best describes management considerations for this patient?
  • A. HBO is contraindicated in pregnancy due to barotrauma risk to the fetus
  • B. Maternal COHb levels directly reflect fetal COHb; if mother is asymptomatic, fetus is unaffected
  • C. HBO is recommended at a lower COHb threshold in pregnancy (>15-20%) because fetal Hb has higher CO affinity and fetal CO elimination is slower
  • D. 100% oxygen via NBO is sufficient for all pregnant patients regardless of COHb level
Fetal hemoglobin has higher CO affinity than adult Hb (fetal Hb oxygen dissociation curve is left-shifted). CO crosses the placenta and fetal COHb can be 10-15% higher than maternal COHb, persisting longer. HBO is recommended at a lower threshold in pregnancy — COHb >15-20% or any neurological symptoms. The COHb elimination half-life in the fetus is significantly longer than in the mother, requiring longer treatment. HBO is considered safe in pregnancy.

End-of-Chapter Assessment: 20 Questions

Q1. What is the most common source of carbon monoxide exposure in North America?
  • A. Industrial chemical synthesis plants
  • B. Combustion in enclosed spaces (fires, malfunctioning furnaces, generators, vehicle exhaust)
  • C. Tobacco cigarette smoking
  • D. Methylene chloride paint stripper inhalation
❌ Incorrect. While industrial CO exposure occurs, it is not the most common source for emergency department presentations.
✅ Correct. Incomplete combustion of carbon-containing fuels in enclosed spaces is the primary source. Generators and vehicles in enclosed garages are particularly dangerous because they produce high CO concentrations rapidly.
❌ Incorrect. Cigarette smoking elevates baseline COHb (to ~10%), but rarely causes acute CO poisoning presentations. Acute CO poisoning is from enclosed-space combustion sources.
❌ Partially correct — methylene chloride is metabolized to CO in vivo and can cause CO poisoning, but it is not the most common source.
Q2. A patient with CO poisoning (COHb 30%) is asymptomatic except for headache after rescue from a structure fire. Why is 100% oxygen treatment critical even with normal PaO2?
  • A. 100% O2 increases PaO2 to enhance dissolved oxygen delivery
  • B. 100% O2 prevents CO from crossing the blood-brain barrier
  • C. 100% O2 competitively displaces CO from hemoglobin and cytochrome c oxidase by mass action, accelerating elimination
  • D. Normal PaO2 indicates CO has been cleared; 100% O2 is only for patients with low PaO2
❌ Incorrect. While dissolved O2 increases slightly, this is not the primary benefit. The main mechanism is mass-action displacement of CO from hemoglobin.
❌ Incorrect. CO is a small gas that freely crosses all membranes. O2 does not prevent CNS penetration — it competes with CO for hemoglobin and cytochrome binding.
✅ Correct. Breathing 100% O2 creates high alveolar O2 tension that competitively displaces CO from hemoglobin (reducing COHb half-life from 5h to 60-90 min) and from cytochrome c oxidase in tissues.
❌ Incorrect. Normal PaO2 in CO poisoning is expected — CO does not impair alveolar gas exchange. COHb can be lethal despite normal PaO2 because oxygen delivery and utilization are impaired at the hemoglobin and cellular level.
Q3. CO poisoning causes tissue hypoxia via which PRIMARY mechanism?
  • A. Binding to hemoglobin with 250x greater affinity than O2, forming COHb and reducing O2-carrying capacity; shifting the ODC left
  • B. Direct pneumotoxicity destroying alveoli and reducing gas exchange
  • C. Peripheral vasodilation causing distributive shock
  • D. Direct cardiac toxicity with pump failure (cardiogenic shock)
✅ Correct. CO's primary toxicity is via hemoglobin — displacing O2 and leftward shift of the dissociation curve (Haldane effect). This reduces both O2 carriage AND tissue O2 delivery.
❌ Incorrect. CO is not directly lung-toxic. Gas exchange (PaO2) is typically normal. The problem is hemoglobin function, not alveolar structure.
❌ Incorrect. While CO can affect vascular tone, distributive shock is not the primary mechanism of tissue hypoxia. COHb-mediated oxygen delivery failure is the primary mechanism.
❌ Incorrect. CO does cause direct cardiac toxicity (cardiac ischemia, arrhythmias) but this is secondary to tissue hypoxia, not the primary mechanism.
Q4. Which neurological symptom in CO poisoning has the BEST correlation with need for hyperbaric oxygen therapy?
  • A. Headache
  • B. Nausea
  • C. Dizziness
  • D. Loss of consciousness (even briefly)
❌ Incorrect. Headache is the most common CO symptom but is not specific and does not independently indicate HBO.
❌ Incorrect. Nausea is common in CO poisoning but is a non-specific symptom that does not independently drive HBO decision-making.
❌ Incorrect. Dizziness is common in CO poisoning but is not the best indicator for HBO compared to LOC and other neurological deficits.
✅ Correct. LOC is the most important historical finding. Any LOC during CO exposure is an accepted HBO indication because it strongly predicts risk for delayed neuropsychiatric syndrome. Even brief LOC correlates with significant CNS involvement.
Q5. A patient with methemoglobinemia from dapsone is treated with methylene blue 2 mg/kg IV. Thirty minutes later, his SpO2 reads 65%, down from 82% before treatment. The nurse is alarmed. What is the most likely explanation?
  • A. Methylene blue worsened methemoglobinemia — administer a second dose immediately
  • B. Methylene blue causes pulse oximetry artifact, reading approximately 65% for 1-2 hours post-administration
  • C. The patient has G6PD deficiency — methylene blue failed and caused hemolysis
  • D. Methylene blue caused bronchospasm, worsening oxygenation
❌ Incorrect. The SpO2 drop is an artifact from methylene blue's optical properties. A second dose is not indicated immediately; clinical assessment and co-oximetry should guide management.
✅ Correct. Methylene blue absorbs at 668 nm (near the red wavelength measured by pulse oximetry), causing SpO2 to read falsely ~65% regardless of true O2 saturation. This is expected and resolves as the drug is metabolized.
❌ Incorrect. While G6PD deficiency causes methylene blue failure and hemolysis, the immediate SpO2 artifact is a pharmacological property of methylene blue itself, not a sign of G6PD deficiency.
❌ Incorrect. Bronchospasm is a rare side effect of rapid methylene blue infusion. The immediate dramatic SpO2 drop immediately after administration is the well-known pulse oximetry artifact.
Q6. A child presents with 'chocolate-brown blood' drawn from an antecubital vein. SpO2 is 81% and PaO2 is 260 mmHg. Which drug is most likely responsible?
  • A. Acetaminophen
  • B. Amoxicillin
  • C. Dapsone
  • D. Ibuprofen
❌ Incorrect. Acetaminophen overdose causes hepatotoxicity, not methemoglobinemia. It does not cause chocolate-brown blood.
❌ Incorrect. Amoxicillin does not cause methemoglobinemia. It is an aminopenicillin antibiotic.
✅ Correct. Dapsone is a sulfone antibiotic well known for causing methemoglobinemia. In pediatric patients on dapsone (e.g., PCP prophylaxis in HIV-infected children), methemoglobinemia is a significant risk. Chocolate-brown blood + SpO2-PaO2 discrepancy = MetHb.
❌ Incorrect. Ibuprofen (NSAID) does not cause methemoglobinemia. It causes GI irritation and rarely nephrotoxicity in overdose.
Q7. Why is cyanide poisoning sometimes called 'histotoxic anoxia' as opposed to 'anemic' or 'hypoxic' anoxia?
  • A. Cells cannot utilize O2 despite normal delivery because cytochrome c oxidase is inhibited by cyanide
  • B. Cyanide reduces hemoglobin oxygen-carrying capacity similar to carbon monoxide
  • C. Cyanide causes pulmonary edema reducing alveolar oxygen transfer
  • D. Cyanide causes peripheral vasodilation reducing tissue perfusion pressure
✅ Correct. 'Histotoxic' = tissue poisoned and unable to use O2. CN⁻ binds Fe³⁺ in cytochrome c oxidase (Complex IV), blocking electron transfer and ATP production. O2 is delivered and present but cannot be used.
❌ Incorrect. Cyanide does not reduce hemoglobin oxygen affinity or capacity (this would be 'anemic anoxia'). Hb-O2 binding is normal in CN poisoning.
❌ Incorrect. Cyanide does not primarily cause pulmonary pathology. Gas exchange (PaO2) is normal. The problem is cellular — mitochondrial electron transport.
❌ Incorrect. While CN poisoning eventually causes cardiovascular collapse, the primary mechanism is not vascular but cellular — electron transport chain inhibition.
Q8. A 55-year-old on nitroprusside infusion for hypertensive emergency develops confusion and lactic acidosis after 72 hours. What is the mechanism and antidote?
  • A. Nitroprusside-induced methemoglobinemia — treat with methylene blue
  • B. Nitroprusside-induced thiocyanate accumulation — treat with dialysis
  • C. Nitroprusside-induced carboxyhemoglobin — treat with 100% oxygen
  • D. Cyanide released from nitroprusside metabolism inhibits cytochrome c oxidase — treat with hydroxocobalamin
❌ Incorrect. Nitroprusside toxicity is cyanide poisoning from CN⁻ release, not methemoglobinemia. Methylene blue would not address CN-mediated cytochrome c oxidase inhibition.
❌ Partially correct — thiocyanate accumulation occurs with prolonged infusion (especially in renal failure) and causes neurotoxicity. However, the acute life-threatening toxicity is from cyanide accumulation with lactic acidosis, not thiocyanate.
❌ Incorrect. Nitroprusside releases cyanide, not carbon monoxide. The toxicity is histotoxic anoxia from CN-mediated electron transport chain inhibition.
✅ Correct. Each nitroprusside molecule contains 5 cyanide groups that are released on metabolism. Accumulation causes cyanide poisoning (histotoxic anoxia, lactic acidosis). Hydroxocobalamin (Cyanokit) chelates CN forming cyanocobalamin.
Q9. Which finding would suggest that a patient with apparent CO poisoning might have concurrent cyanide poisoning (as in smoke inhalation victims)?
  • A. COHb >25%
  • B. Lactic acidosis (lactate >10 mmol/L) despite adequate oxygenation and 100% O2 treatment
  • C. Pulse oximetry reading of 92%
  • D. Cherry-red skin coloration
❌ Incorrect. High COHb confirms CO poisoning but does not indicate concurrent cyanide. Many fire victims have high COHb without clinically significant cyanide poisoning.
✅ Correct. Severe lactic acidosis (>10 mmol/L) in a smoke inhalation victim disproportionate to their apparent oxygenation status suggests concurrent cyanide poisoning (histotoxic anoxia prevents cellular O2 use despite adequate delivery). CO alone rarely causes this degree of lactic acidosis.
❌ Incorrect. SpO2 is unreliable in CO poisoning (reads falsely normal or as 85% if MetHb present). It is not useful for detecting concurrent cyanide poisoning.
❌ Incorrect. Cherry-red skin is associated with CO poisoning (from oxygenated COHb). It is not specific for concurrent cyanide poisoning. In practice, cherry-red skin is seen post-mortem more than clinically.
Q10. A 19-year-old uses a topical anesthetic spray (benzocaine) before performing oral self-surgery. He presents with cyanosis that doesn't improve with 15L O2. SpO2 is 83%. What is the diagnosis and initial treatment?
  • A. Anaphylaxis to benzocaine — give epinephrine 0.3 mg IM
  • B. CO poisoning from combustion during procedure — give 100% O2
  • C. Methemoglobinemia from benzocaine absorption — methylene blue 1-2 mg/kg IV
  • D. Tension pneumothorax — needle decompression at 2nd intercostal space
❌ Incorrect. Anaphylaxis presents with urticaria, bronchospasm, and hypotension — not the SpO2 plateau at 83% despite 15L O2 which is characteristic of MetHb.
❌ Incorrect. SpO2 in CO poisoning reads falsely NORMAL (98-99%), not 83%. The 83% SpO2 plateau with cyanosis is MetHb pattern. There is no combustion source described.
✅ Correct. Benzocaine causes MetHb, especially from mucosal application. SpO2 plateau at ~83% despite high-flow O2 confirms MetHb (cannot read higher due to MetHb optical properties). Methylene blue reverses MetHb via NADPH-dependent pathway.
❌ Incorrect. Tension pneumothorax presents with absent breath sounds, tracheal deviation, and hypotension. The SpO2 pattern (plateau at 83% unresponsive to O2) is specific for dyshemoglobinemia, not pneumothorax.
Q11. What is the mechanism by which methylene blue treats methemoglobinemia?
  • A. Methylene blue is reduced by NADPH (via G6PD/HMP shunt) to leukomethylene blue, which reduces MetHb (Fe³⁺) back to Hb (Fe²⁺)
  • B. Methylene blue oxidizes MetHb from Fe³⁺ to Fe⁴⁺, then spontaneous reduction to Fe²⁺ occurs
  • C. Methylene blue chelates the ferric iron in MetHb, releasing it from hemoglobin
  • D. Methylene blue activates hemoglobin methemoglobin reductase directly without cofactors
✅ Correct. The G6PD/HMP shunt generates NADPH → reduces MB to leuco-MB → leuco-MB reduces Fe³⁺ MetHb to Fe²⁺ Hb. This is why G6PD deficiency renders methylene blue ineffective.
❌ Incorrect. Methylene blue acts as an electron acceptor (is reduced) to then donate electrons to MetHb (reducing it). The oxidation step is MB being reduced, not MetHb being further oxidized.
❌ Incorrect. Methylene blue is not a chelator. It reduces MetHb through an electron transfer mechanism, not chelation.
❌ Incorrect. Methylene blue REQUIRES NADPH as a cofactor (from G6PD). It cannot activate the reductase pathway independently.
Q12. A house fire victim arrives with COHb 42%. After 90 minutes of 100% NBO, COHb has decreased to 18%. She has no neurological symptoms. Does this patient require hyperbaric oxygen?
  • A. No — the current COHb of 18% is below the HBO threshold; discharge after 6 hours of NBO
  • B. Yes — initial COHb 42% meets HBO criteria; HBO should be considered if accessible to reduce delayed neurological syndrome risk
  • C. Only if a repeat ECG shows ST-segment changes
  • D. Only for patients with COHb >50% — 42% does not meet HBO criteria
❌ Incorrect. The initial COHb of 42% met HBO criteria. Serial COHb levels alone do not determine HBO necessity — the initial severity, symptom history, and ongoing risk of delayed neurological syndrome must be considered.
✅ Correct. HBO criteria are based on the initial presentation, not just the current COHb after NBO treatment. COHb 42% initially meets most HBO criteria. HBO may reduce the risk of delayed neuropsychiatric syndrome even after apparent clinical improvement.
❌ Incorrect. Cardiac monitoring is important in severe CO poisoning, but HBO decisions are based primarily on COHb levels, neurological symptoms, and clinical criteria — not contingent on ECG changes alone.
❌ Incorrect. Most accepted HBO criteria use thresholds of COHb >25% or clinical criteria (LOC, neurological symptoms). COHb 42% clearly meets these thresholds.
Q13. A patient with cyanide poisoning is treated with sodium nitrite 300 mg IV. What is the primary mechanism of sodium nitrite's antidotal action?
  • A. Sodium nitrite chelates cyanide directly, forming a water-soluble complex
  • B. Sodium nitrite produces methemoglobin, which has high CN affinity and acts as a CN sink away from cytochrome c oxidase
  • C. Sodium nitrite enhances renal cyanide clearance by alkalinizing urine
  • D. Sodium nitrite directly activates cytochrome c oxidase, bypassing cyanide inhibition
❌ Incorrect. Sodium nitrite does not chelate cyanide directly. It produces methemoglobin, which then acts as the cyanide acceptor.
✅ Correct. MetHb competes with cytochrome c oxidase for CN binding, removing CN from the mitochondria. The CN-MetHb complex then donates CN to sodium thiosulfate for conversion to thiocyanate.
❌ Incorrect. Sodium nitrite's mechanism is hemoglobin oxidation to MetHb. Renal clearance of CN is enhanced via the thiosulfate step (forming thiocyanate), not urine alkalinization.
❌ Incorrect. Sodium nitrite cannot reactivate blocked cytochrome c oxidase directly. The mechanism is indirect — producing MetHb to sequester CN away from the enzyme.
Q14. Why is hydroxocobalamin (Cyanokit) preferred over the nitrite-thiosulfate combination for cyanide poisoning in fire victims?
  • A. Sodium nitrite produces MetHb which worsens oxygen carrying capacity when CO is also reducing Hb function; hydroxocobalamin chelates CN without causing MetHb
  • B. Hydroxocobalamin has faster onset than nitrite-thiosulfate
  • C. Nitrite-thiosulfate requires IV access but hydroxocobalamin can be given IM
  • D. Hydroxocobalamin is only used for pediatric patients; nitrite-thiosulfate for adults
✅ Correct. In fire victims with CO + CN poisoning, the combined COHb (CO) + MetHb (nitrite) + CN toxicity would critically reduce functional hemoglobin. Hydroxocobalamin avoids this by chelating CN directly.
❌ Incorrect. Onset is rapid with both regimens. The key advantage of hydroxocobalamin is safety (no MetHb production), not necessarily faster onset.
❌ Incorrect. Both antidotes require IV administration. Route of administration is not the distinguishing factor.
❌ Incorrect. Hydroxocobalamin is used for both adults and children. Dosing differs by weight.
Q15. A 70-year-old with G6PD deficiency develops severe methemoglobinemia (MetHb 55%) from dapsone. Methylene blue 2 mg/kg IV is given with no improvement. What is the most appropriate next step?
  • A. Increase methylene blue to 10 mg/kg IV
  • B. Administer sodium nitrite to provide alternative MetHb reduction pathway
  • C. Ascorbic acid (Vitamin C) 2g IV as definitive treatment
  • D. Exchange transfusion to replace MetHb-containing blood with functional hemoglobin
❌ Incorrect. In G6PD deficiency, methylene blue fails because NADPH is not available. Higher doses will not work and paradoxically, very high methylene blue doses can CAUSE methemoglobinemia.
❌ Incorrect. Sodium nitrite CAUSES methemoglobinemia by oxidizing Hb. Giving it to a patient with severe MetHb would worsen toxicity.
❌ Incorrect. Ascorbic acid is an alternative that slowly reduces MetHb via a G6PD-independent pathway. However, for severe MetHb (55%) that requires rapid reversal, ascorbic acid is too slow. Exchange transfusion is more appropriate.
✅ Correct. Exchange transfusion replaces the patient's blood (containing high MetHb) with donor RBCs containing normal hemoglobin. This is the definitive treatment when methylene blue fails (G6PD deficiency) and MetHb is severely elevated.
Q16. What is the 'saturation gap' in dyshemoglobinemia and how is it clinically applied?
  • A. The gap between PaO2 and alveolar PAO2, indicating pulmonary shunting
  • B. The difference between SpO2 before and after administering supplemental O2
  • C. Discrepancy between pulse oximetry SpO2 and co-oximetry true saturation, indicating dyshemoglobin (COHb or MetHb) is present
  • D. The gap between arterial and venous O2 saturation reflecting tissue O2 extraction
❌ Incorrect. The A-a gradient (PaO2 vs. PAO2) reflects pulmonary gas exchange. The 'saturation gap' in dyshemoglobinemia specifically refers to the discrepancy between SpO2 (pulse ox) and true O2 saturation (co-oximetry).
❌ Incorrect. While the response to O2 provides clinical information, the 'saturation gap' specifically describes the SpO2 vs. co-oximetry discrepancy indicating dyshemoglobins are present.
✅ Correct. When SpO2 reads higher than expected (normal in CO poisoning) or reads ~85% despite high-flow O2 (MetHb), the gap between SpO2 and co-oximetry-measured SaO2 indicates dyshemoglobin. This gap drives the clinical diagnosis.
❌ Incorrect. The arteriovenous O2 difference reflects tissue extraction. In cyanide poisoning, this gap is paradoxically narrow (arterialization of venous blood), but this is different from the 'saturation gap' concept.
Q17. A patient presents with co-existing CO poisoning (COHb 22%) and methemoglobinemia (MetHb 18%). How does this combination particularly dangerous?
  • A. Both reduce functional Hb available for O2 transport additively; combined effect is greater than either alone
  • B. CO and MetHb cancel each other out, making the combination less dangerous
  • C. The combination uniquely causes irreversible hemoglobin denaturation
  • D. MetHb blocks CO from binding hemoglobin, reducing CO toxicity
✅ Correct. COHb + MetHb additively reduce functional oxyHb. With CO 22% + MetHb 18%, only ~60% of Hb carries O2. Both also left-shift the ODC, impairing O2 delivery. Treatment requires 100% O2 (for CO) AND methylene blue (for MetHb).
❌ Incorrect. They do not cancel each other — they both act to reduce functional hemoglobin and are additive in their toxic effects.
❌ Incorrect. Both CO and MetHb cause reversible hemoglobin dysfunction (treated with O2 and methylene blue respectively). Neither causes irreversible denaturation at these levels.
❌ Incorrect. MetHb and COHb are separate hemoglobin-bound species and do not prevent each other's formation. They bind to different molecules of hemoglobin.
Q18. Which of the following agents does NOT cause methemoglobinemia?
  • A. Dapsone
  • B. Benzocaine (topical anesthetic)
  • C. Sodium nitrite
  • D. Carbon monoxide
❌ Incorrect (DOES cause MetHb). Dapsone is one of the most common drug-related causes of methemoglobinemia, especially with chronic use.
❌ Incorrect (DOES cause MetHb). Benzocaine is a well-documented cause of MetHb, particularly via mucosal application.
❌ Incorrect (DOES cause MetHb). Sodium nitrite is used therapeutically to intentionally produce MetHb as a cyanide antidote, demonstrating its oxidizing effect on hemoglobin.
✅ Correct. CO forms COHb by binding to Fe²⁺ without oxidizing it to Fe³⁺ — so it does NOT cause methemoglobinemia. CO and MetHb are different types of dyshemoglobin through different mechanisms.
Q19. A patient with CO poisoning has a COHb of 15% and complains only of headache after removal from the source. ECG shows no changes. What is the appropriate initial treatment and expected COHb elimination time?
  • A. Room air observation at home for 24 hours
  • B. 100% O2 via non-rebreather mask for 4-6 hours; COHb will normalize in approximately 4-6 hours
  • C. Immediate hyperbaric oxygen at 2.5 ATA for 90 minutes
  • D. IV N-acetylcysteine (NAC) to prevent delayed neurological syndrome
❌ Incorrect. 100% O2 is needed to accelerate CO elimination. Sending the patient home on room air is inappropriate — half-life on room air is ~5 hours and delayed neurological effects need monitoring.
✅ Correct. NBO reduces COHb half-life to ~60-90 minutes. From 15% baseline, 3-4 half-lives would reduce COHb to normal levels in approximately 4-6 hours. ED observation during treatment is appropriate.
❌ Incorrect. HBO is not indicated for mild CO poisoning (headache only, COHb 15%, no LOC, no neurological symptoms). NBO for 4-6 hours is appropriate.
❌ Incorrect. NAC has no established role in CO poisoning. It is used for acetaminophen toxicity. No specific medication beyond O2 therapy is standard for CO poisoning.
Q20. Which of the following is most accurate regarding the delayed neurological syndrome (DNS) of CO poisoning?
  • A. DNS only occurs with COHb levels above 50%
  • B. DNS presents immediately as the patient awakens after CO poisoning
  • C. DNS occurs 2-40 days after apparent recovery and includes cognitive impairment, personality changes, and Parkinsonism
  • D. DNS is fully reversible within 1 week with high-dose corticosteroids
❌ Incorrect. DNS can occur with any significant CO poisoning. COHb levels don't perfectly predict DNS risk — it is more closely associated with LOC and clinical severity, not just COHb level.
❌ Incorrect. DNS is defined by its DELAYED onset — symptoms appear 2-40 days after apparent recovery (the 'lucid interval'). Immediate symptoms are part of the acute episode, not DNS.
✅ Correct. DNS (sometimes called 'delayed neuropsychiatric syndrome') has the characteristic delayed onset 2-40 days after recovery, affecting 10-30% of severe CO poisoning cases. HBO may reduce risk but does not eliminate it.
❌ Incorrect. DNS is not reliably reversed by corticosteroids. Some patients recover partially or fully over months, but recovery is variable and corticosteroids have no established role.
